l: Mercury's mission to kill Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter sends Mercury to put Argus to death because Io's suffering can no longer be endured. Mercury approaches Argus disguised as a shepherd and tries to overpower his watchful eyes with the sound of his pipes and extended conversation.

l: Pan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pan falls in love with Syrinx and pursues her as she returns from the hill of Lycæus. When he thinks he has caught her, he seizes reeds instead of her body; charmed by their sound, he joins them with wax into an instrument.

l: Syrinx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Syrinx is a famous Naiad among the Hamadryads of Nonacris who values her virginity and follows the Ortygian Goddess. She flees from Pan, asks the Naiads for help at the river Ladon, and is changed into reeds.

l: the Naiads, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Naiads are Syrinx's watery sisters. When the river Ladon stops Syrinx's flight, she invokes their aid, and they change her into reeds.

l: the river Ladon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The sandy river Ladon stops Syrinx as she flees from Pan.

l: instrument (Pan's), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The panpipes are made from unequal reeds joined together with wax. Pan makes them after hearing the wind produce a murmuring, sweet sound among the reeds, and they retain Syrinx's name.

l: the reeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The reeds are what Pan seizes when he believes he has caught Syrinx. Wind moving among them produces a murmuring sound, and Pan joins unequal reeds with wax to make an instrument.

l: Syrinx's flight, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Pan's pursuit of Syrinx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pan pursues Syrinx after falling in love with her. He follows her from the hill of Lycæus until she reaches the river Ladon, where he thinks he has caught her but grasps reeds instead.

l: Syrinx's transformation into reeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: When Syrinx is stopped by the river Ladon, she asks the Naiads to change her. They transform her into reeds, which Pan later uses to make his instrument.

l: the invention of the panpipes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: peacock (Juno's bird), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Io is driven by Juno’s Fury and invisible stings to wander through the whole earth. She reaches the Nile, begs through groans, tears, and mournful lowing for an end to her suffering, and is later restored to human form and worshipped as a goddess in Egypt.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Juno sends a dreadful Fury before Io and drives her, terrified and maddened, across the earth. She is eventually pacified and agrees to end Io’s punishment.

l: Nile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Nile remains the utmost boundary of Io’s long wanderings. When Io reaches it, she falls at its bank and appeals toward Heaven.

l: Egypt, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Egypt is where Io’s wandering ends and where she is worshipped as a goddess by a linen-wearing throng.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter embraces Juno and entreats her to end Io’s punishment, promising that Io will never again trouble her. He swears this by calling the Stygian waters to hear the oath, and Epaphus is believed to have been born from his seed.

l: Epaphus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Epaphus is believed to have been born to Io from the seed of great Jupiter. He possesses temples joined to those of his parent and mocks Phaëton for believing his mother and claiming an imaginary father.

l: Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Sun is identified by Clymene as Phaëton’s father and as the power that governs the world. Its dwelling is said to be close to Clymene’s region, and Phaëton journeys toward it.

l: Clymene, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Clymene hears Phaëton’s account of Epaphus’s reproaches and confirms by an oath that Phaëton was begotten by the Sun. She tells him that he can visit the Sun’s dwelling and inquire of the Sun himself.

l: Io's restoration to human form, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Io's worship as Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening

l: Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Isis is the name under which Io is worshipped in Egypt after Juno permits her restoration and she regains her human form.

l: Io's wandering, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Io’s wandering is caused by Juno’s Fury and invisible stings, which drive her in fright through the whole earth. The wandering ends when she reaches the Nile in Egypt.

l: Phaëton's journey to the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: After Clymene confirms that the Sun is his father, Phaëton immediately travels toward the Sun’s dwelling. He passes his own Æthiopians and the Indians beneath the Sun’s rays while heading toward the rising of the Sun.

The ride brings destructive fire to the earth, rivers, seas, and heavens, and Earth begs the ruler of the gods to stop it.

l: Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.
s: Earth is scorched as Phaëton’s uncontrolled chariot brings fire across her surface. She sees her vegetation, cities, mountains, rivers, seas, and inhabitants threatened, and begs the ruler of the gods to save the universe.

l: Sun's palace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.

l: the Sun's chariot, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.
s: Phaëton’s chariot is a magnificent vehicle made by Vulcan, with a golden axle, poles, and wheel rim, silver spokes, and jewels set along the yoke. Because Phaëton is too light to provide its usual burden, it becomes unstable and bounds through the air.

l: the horses (Phaëton's chariot), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.
s: The Sun horses, Pyroeis, Eoüs, Æthon, and Phlegon, are fiery, winged steeds that are difficult to restrain. After sensing the chariot’s unusual lightness, they leave the regular track and run wherever their fury carries them.

l: Phaëton's failed chariot ride, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.
s: Phaëton cannot control the horses or recognize the route, and he eventually drops the reins when he sees the threatening Scorpion. The chariot then travels through unknown regions of the sky, alternately rising high and plunging near the earth.

l: flames, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.

l: world's destruction, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, BOOK THE SECOND.
s: The world suffers widespread destruction as nations, cities, forests, mountains, rivers, and seas are scorched or dried up. l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Phaëton's failed chariot ride, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Phaëton’s conflagration, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening .. opening

s: The Hesperian Naiads are identified as the Naiads of Italy, named Phaëthusa, Lampetie, and Phœbe.

l: the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes

l: the sun having stood still upon Gibeon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes

s: The shadow returning ten degrees backward is presented as a possible faint reference to the time when the shadow moved backward by the sun-dial of Ahaz.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cycnus, king of the Ligurians and related to Phaëton, mourns Phaëton’s death beside the Eridanus and is transformed into a swan. l: Cycnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cycnus, king of the Ligurians and related to Phaëton, leaves his kingdom to mourn Phaëton beside the Eridanus and in the wood augmented by the sisters. His human voice becomes shrill, gray feathers cover his hair, and he is transformed into a new bird.

l: Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Phaëton is mourned intensely by Cycnus, who is related to him on his mother’s side and more closely allied to him in affection. His death causes his father to grieve, grow resentful, and blame the flame-footed steeds.

l: Cycnus's transformation into a swan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Cycnus’s transformation changes his voice, hair, neck, feet, sides, and mouth: feathers appear, his neck lengthens, a membrane joins his reddening toes, and his mouth becomes a bill without a point. The transformation makes him a bird that avoids the heavens, air, and fire and instead frequents pools, lakes, and streams.

l: swan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The swan is the new form taken by Cycnus. It avoids the heavens and the air because of the fire sent from there and chooses streams, pools, and wide lakes instead.

l: Phaëton's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Phaëton’s death leaves Cycnus inconsolable and drives him to abandon his kingdom and mourn beside the Eridanus. It also causes Phaëton’s father to reject his labor and blame the flame-footed steeds.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The father of Phaëton appears in squalid clothing and without his usual comeliness, as during an eclipse. He grieves, resents what happened, refuses to provide his services to the world, and challenges Jupiter or another God to drive the chariot carrying the light.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Phœbus calls together the flame-footed steeds, which remain maddened and trembling with terror. He subdues them with whip and lash, vents his fury, upbraids them with Phaëton’s death, and charges them with causing it.

l: the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Sun’s father is described as suffering an eclipse of his disk when he is squalid and deprived of his comeliness. He is unwilling to continue driving the chariot that carries the light after Phaëton’s death.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter excuses the hurling of his lightnings and adds threats to the Gods’ entreaties that darkness not be brought over the world. Phaëton’s father challenges Jupiter to drive the chariot so that he may experience the strength of the flame-footed steeds.

l: the horses (Phaëton's chariot), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The flame-footed steeds are maddened and still trembling with terror after Phaëton’s death. Phœbus subdues them with whip and lash, angrily reproaches them, and blames them for Phaëton’s death.

l: the fire, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The fire is associated with the heavens and is remembered by Cycnus as having been unjustly sent from there. Cycnus, in his new bird form, abhors fire and chooses streams as its opposite.

l: Phaëton's sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: the poplars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: amber, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Cycnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: swan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Phaëton and his sisters tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The tradition says that Phaëton’s sisters died from grief near his tomb and were changed into trees that distilled amber. Lucian said that the inhabitants near the river Po did not know this tradition.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter surveys the world after the fire and sees Calisto, a virgin of Nonacris and devoted follower of Diana, in Arcadia. He assumes Diana’s form to approach her, then embraces and assaults her despite her resistance. Calisto returns to Diana’s company ashamed, and the Nymphs notice signs of what has happened. During a later bathing, her pregnancy is exposed, so Diana drives her from the sacred springs and orders her to leave the train.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter sees Calisto while surveying the restored earth and desires her. He assumes the form and dress of Diana, deceives Calisto, and assaults her despite her resistance before returning to heaven.

l: Calisto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Calisto is a virgin of Nonacris and a favored follower of Diana, skilled in hunting and devoted to chastity. After Jupiter assaults her, she returns ashamed and later has her pregnancy exposed when Diana’s company bathes.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Diana encounters Calisto again with her Nymphs and notices that Calisto’s behavior has changed, though her virginity prevents her from recognizing the cause immediately. When Calisto’s pregnancy is exposed during bathing, Diana orders her to leave the sacred springs and drives her from the company.

l: the Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Nymphs notice signs of Calisto’s injured honor when she returns to Diana’s company. They later bathe with Diana and witness the exposure of Calisto’s pregnancy.

l: the violation of Calisto's vow of chastity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Calisto’s vow of chastity is violated when Jupiter, disguised as Diana, embraces and assaults her. The violation becomes evident through her shame, altered behavior, and eventual pregnancy.

l: Jupiter's seduction and assault of Calisto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Jupiter’s deception begins when he assumes Diana’s appearance and approaches Calisto as one of Diana’s companions. He kisses and embraces her, prevents her from resisting, and assaults her before leaving the grove.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Juno transforms Calisto into a bear after learning that she has borne Jupiter’s son, Arcas. l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Juno, jealous of Calisto’s relationship with Jupiter and the birth of Arcas, transforms Calisto into a bear. After Calisto is placed among the stars, Juno angrily asks Tethys and Ocean to exclude the new constellations from their waters.

l: Calisto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Calisto is transformed by Juno from a human into a bear, while retaining her former understanding. She later encounters her son Arcas, who does not recognize her, and is placed among the stars by Jupiter.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Jupiter is identified as Calisto’s lover and the father of Arcas. He prevents Arcas from killing the bear who is his mother and places Calisto and Arcas in the heavens.

l: Arcas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Arcas, the son of Calisto and Jupiter, grows up without recognizing his transformed mother. While hunting, he is about to pierce her with a spear, but Jupiter removes them both to the heavens.

l: Bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Great Bear is identified with the constellation formed when Jupiter places Calisto among the stars. The explanation says that its never setting may have inspired Juno’s request that it not be received into the Ocean.

l: Little Bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Little Bear is identified with the constellation formed when Jupiter places Arcas among the stars. The explanation suggests that Arcas’s early death may have been the origin of this constellation.

l: raven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The raven was formerly white and was praised for its beautiful feathers. Because of its garrulous tongue and the report it carried, it is changed to a bird with black wings.

l: Coronis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Coronis, a woman from Larissa in Hæmonia, is described as exceptionally beautiful and as having pleased the Delphian God while she remained chaste. Her infidelity is discovered and reported by the bird of Phoebus.

l: Heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The heavens receive Calisto and Arcas as neighboring constellations after Jupiter carries them through the air. Juno resents Calisto’s elevation and notes that the former mistress has been made a goddess.

l: transformation of Calisto into a bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Juno seizes Calisto by the hair and throws her to the ground, where her arms grow black hair, her hands become hooked claws, and her mouth becomes that of a bear. Calisto retains her human understanding but loses the power of speech.

l: placement of Calisto and Arcas among the stars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: When Arcas is about to kill Calisto without recognizing her, Jupiter prevents the act and carries both of them into the heavens. He makes them neighboring constellations.

l: the raven's transformation from white to black, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The raven’s white plumage becomes black as punishment for its prattling and disclosure of hidden matters. The text presents its tongue as the cause of the change in color.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: A virgin who is Apollo's favorite tells Minerva how her fidelity led to her punishment and how she became a crow. Minerva entrusted Ericthonius, who was born without a mother, to Pandrosos, Herse, and Aglauros in a basket, forbidding them to investigate its secret; Aglauros opened it and saw a child with a dragon beside him. The virgin reported this to Minerva but was banished from her protection and placed after the bird of the night. She also explains that the God of the Ocean pursued and attempted to assault her before a virgin transformed her into a bird, and she resents being replaced in honor by Nyctimene.

l: virgin (Apollo's favorite; later changed into a crow), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The virgin watches the three virgins entrusted with Ericthonius and reports Aglauros's discovery to Minerva. She says that she is Apollo's favorite, that she was the daughter of Coroneus, and that she was a virgin of royal birth before being changed into a crow.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minerva encloses Ericthonius in a basket and entrusts him to three virgins with instructions not to investigate her secret. After the virgin reports Aglauros's disobedience, Minerva banishes the virgin from her protection.

l: Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ericthonius is described as an offspring born without a mother. Minerva encloses him in a basket and gives it to three virgins to keep.

l: the three virgins entrusted with Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Pandrosos, Herse, and Aglauros are entrusted by Minerva with keeping the basket containing Ericthonius. Pandrosos and Herse observe their charge without treachery, while Aglauros opens the basket despite Minerva's injunction.

l: Aglauros, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Aglauros calls her sisters cowards and unties the knots of the basket. She and her sisters then see a child with a dragon extended beside him.

l: God of the Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The God of the Ocean sees the virgin walking along the sea-shore and becomes inflamed with desire. After his entreaties fail, he prepares to use violence and follows her as she flees.

l: Nyctimene, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Nyctimene is described as having been made a bird for a horrid crime. The virgin says that Nyctimene has succeeded her in honor.

l: basket containing Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minerva makes the basket from Actæan twigs and gives it to Pandrosos, Herse, and Aglauros. She orders them not to inquire into its secret, but Aglauros unties its knots and looks inside.

l: dragon beside Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: When Aglauros opens the basket, the three virgins see a child and a dragon extended beside him.

l: crow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The virgin is changed into a crow and is placed after the bird of the night. She says that her punishment may warn birds not to incur dangers through their chattering.

l: the basket's secret, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Minerva forbids the three virgins to investigate the basket's secret. Its contents are revealed when Aglauros opens it: a child and a dragon beside him.

l: fidelity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The virgin says that her fidelity was her ruin because she reported Aglauros's discovery to Minerva. She presents the report as an act of loyalty rather than treachery.

l: the crow's punishment and banishment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: For telling Minerva what Aglauros had done, the virgin is said to have been banished from Minerva's protection and placed after the bird of the night. Her punishment is connected with her chattering about what she had seen.

l: the attempted assault by the God of the Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The God of the Ocean pursues the virgin along the shore after she rejects his soft words and attempts to use violence. She flees across the yielding sand and invokes gods and men, but no mortal hears her.

l: the virgin's transformation into a crow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: As the virgin raises her arms toward heaven, they grow black with light feathers, and her garments become feathers rooted in her skin. Her hands and breast change, she runs without being slowed by the sand, and she is lifted into the air and assigned to Minerva as a faultless companion.

l: Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

He was also credited with instituting the Panathenæa, and Hyginus says that after his death he became the constellation Auriga, the Charioteer.

l: Amphictyon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Amphictyon disputed the right to the crown of Athens with Ericthonius after Cranaus’s death. One account says Amphictyon initially prevailed but was later succeeded by Ericthonius, while Apollodorus says that Ericthonius dethroned him.

l: Athens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Athens was the kingdom whose crown was disputed by Ericthonius and Amphictyon. Ericthonius is said to have instituted the festival of the Panathenæa there.

l: Panathenæa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Panathenæa was a festival that Ericthonius was said to have instituted at Athens. In time, it was adopted by the whole of Greece.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Nyctimene is transformed into an owl after defiling the bed of her father, and she avoids human gaze and daylight. The raven tells Apollo that Coronis has been unfaithful with a youth of Hæmonia. He rescues their unborn child from the funeral flames and carries the child to the cave of the two-formed Chiron, while banishing the raven from the white birds.

l: Nyctimene, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Nyctimene defiled the bed of her father and was transformed into a bird. Conscious of her crime, she avoids human gaze and daylight, hides in darkness, and is expelled from the sky by the other birds.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo hears the raven’s report about Coronis and kills Coronis with an arrow. He later regrets his vengeance, blames himself for listening to the raven, performs Coronis’s obsequies, rescues their child from the flames, and forbids the raven to perch among the white birds.

l: Coronis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Coronis is reported to have lain with a youth of Hæmonia. Apollo wounds her with an arrow; before dying, she says that she might have been punished after first giving birth, and that she and the child will die together.

l: raven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The raven reports to Apollo that Coronis has been unfaithful. Apollo blames the raven for revealing the cause of his sorrow and forbids it to remain among the white birds.

l: Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Coronis’s child is still in her womb when Apollo kills her. Apollo snatches the child from the flames and from the womb of its mother and carries it to the cave of the two-formed Chiron.

l: incest, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The incest concerns Nyctimene’s criminal passion for and defilement of the bed of her father. The Gods punish it by transforming Nyctimene into an owl.

l: Coronis's infidelity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Coronis’s infidelity consists of lying down with a youth of Hæmonia. The raven tells Apollo about it, leading Apollo to kill Coronis.

l: Nyctimene's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods transform Nyctimene into an owl as punishment for her incest. Afterward, she avoids light and human gaze and is expelled from the sky by the other birds.

l: Coronis's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Apollo pierces Coronis’s breast with an arrow. She removes the steel, bathes her white limbs in blood, speaks her final words, and dies as a deadly coldness takes her body.

l: Coronis's funeral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: A funeral pile is prepared for Coronis, and her limbs are about to be burned. Apollo pours perfumes on her breast, embraces her, performs the due obsequies, and removes the child from the flames.

l: the raven's report, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The raven’s report tells Apollo that he has seen Coronis lying down with a youth of Hæmonia. Apollo listens to the report, kills Coronis, and later blames the raven for causing his sorrow.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes

l: Coronis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Coronis is described as a Nymph whose name was also used for a crow. The story says that she was transformed into a crow for making too faithful a report.

l: virgin (Apollo's favorite; later changed into a crow), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The crow is the form into which Coronis was transformed for making too faithful a report. Lucian and other writers fabled that Æsculapius was produced from the egg of this bird.

l: raven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The raven was changed from white to black for talking too much.

l: the virgin's transformation into a crow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fable says that Coronis was transformed into a crow as punishment for making too faithful a report. The explanation states that history offers no insight into the foundation of this story.

l: the raven's transformation from white to black, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fable says that the raven changed from white to black for talking too much. The explanation states that history offers no insight into the foundation of this story.

l: Fables, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: The Fables about Coronis and the raven may refer to events involving two persons entirely unknown to history. They perhaps concern persons who lived as far back as the time of the daughters of Cecrops, to whom the stories seem to bear some relation.

l: Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, notes .. notes
s: Æsculapius is identified as the son of Coronis. Lucian and other writers fabled that he was produced from the egg of the crow and born in the shape of a serpent, under which form he was very generally worshipped.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ocyrrhoe, daughter of the Centaur Chiron, prophesies the future of the infant Æsculapius and the fate of her father. She also predicts that Chiron will eventually become subject to death after being wounded by a baneful serpent’s blood. Before she can say more, Ocyrrhoe is transformed into a mare and given the new name Enippe.

l: Ocyrrhoë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ocyrrhoe, the daughter of Chiron and Chariclo, learns her father’s arts and sings the secrets of the Fates. She prophesies the fates of Æsculapius and Chiron, but the Fates prevent her from speaking further; she is then transformed into a mare and named Enippe.

l: Chiron, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Chiron is proud of his pupil of divine origin and rejoices in the responsibility. Ocyrrhoe prophesies that although he is immortal, he will later wish to die after receiving the blood of a baneful serpent in his wounded limbs, and that the Gods will make him subject to death.

l: Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Æsculapius is an infant of divine origin whom Ocyrrhoe foretells will become the giver of health to the whole world. He will restore life to the dead, be hindered by the bolts of his grandsire after doing so against the will of the Gods, and become a God again after becoming a lifeless carcase.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Gods are associated with Æsculapius’s power to restore life and with the prohibition against doing so against their will. They transform Ocyrrhoe from a human shape into a mare, and they make Chiron, who was immortal, subject to death.

l: Fates, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: The Fates prevent Ocyrrhoe from saying anything more about the future. They are also described as the three Goddesses who will cut Chiron’s threads.

l: Ocyrrhoe's transformation into a mare, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
s: Ocyrrhoe’s human shape withdraws as she desires grass and wishes to range over the plains. Her fingers join into a hoof, her face and neck lengthen, much of her hair becomes a tail, and the remaining hair becomes a mane; her voice and shape change, and she receives the name Enippe.

l: prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, opening
